question: How does the owner's sentence 'Version 2 of the PRD supersedes version 1 together with update 1' change the run's sources?

options.label: PRD v2 normative; PRD v1 and update 1 baseline; RFC-001 stays normative
options.consequence: Specs cite PRD v2 for product scope; RFC-001 keeps governing the accepted technical choices it covers (session model, password storage, stacks) until an ADR of this run supersedes a part of it; the old PRD and update stay readable as history.

options.label: PRD v2 normative; PRD v1, update 1 and RFC-001 all baseline
options.consequence: Every technical choice of RFC-001 would need re-deciding or an ADR restating it, although PRD v2 changes none of them except persistence and the endpoint count.

chosen: PRD v2 normative; PRD v1 and update 1 baseline; RFC-001 stays normative
why: The sentence names the PRD and update 1 only. PRD v2 restates stories 1 to 3 and adds stories 4 to 6, so v1 and update 1 have no content v2 lacks. RFC-001 is the accepted technical approach for sign-in and profile, which PRD v2 keeps; its 'no database' and 'exactly two endpoints' statements follow from PRD v1's scope and are overtaken by PRD v2's Constraints and Scope, which the intake step will route. A later RFC from the team would have changed this choice.

question: How do the owner's sentences 'take it in end to end, through every handoff the intake record names' and 'Decide and record every question; I review the decisions afterwards in one sitting' change how the run behaves?

options.label: No scope limit; stop policy decide-and-record, which run.yaml already sets
options.consequence: The segment runs every handoff and answers every stop-set class as a recorded decision with would_have_asked true; only hard stops end it.

options.label: Read 'every question' as also removing stop-set classes
options.consequence: Same behavior under decide-and-record, since the stop set only matters under the stop policy; removing classes would lose the would_have_asked labels the owner reviews.

chosen: No scope limit; stop policy decide-and-record, which run.yaml already sets
why: The instruction asks for the whole intake and for answers instead of questions, which is exactly decide-and-record; the stop set stays whole so every answer given on the owner's behalf is labelled for the review sitting.

options.label: Record that enforcement starts with the next host session; launch with the default agent type now
options.consequence: For this session the deny rules and the Bash hook are prompt instructions only; the gate checks every write after the fact.

options.label: Stop and ask the owner to restart the session

chosen: Record that enforcement starts with the next host session; launch with the default agent type now

options.label: Stop until the owner starts a session in this repository
options.consequence: The run waits for a human; the tutorial records a cleaner launch but nothing else changes.

chosen: One extra launch-prompt line naming the repository root, and one cited context line per dispatch telling the step to read the skill's SKILL.md under .claude/skills by path
why: The builder's smoke run used the same two deviations and reached DONE; neither changes what a step reads or writes. A session started in this repository would remove both.

question: Classify, one class per intake: local, cross-node, new-capability or structural?

options.label: cross-node
options.consequence: The existing root and its three leaf-parents take the change: ADR and contract handoffs first, then node touches, then phases appended on backend, web and integration. No node is added and the tree keeps its shape.

options.label: new-capability
options.consequence: A booking node (or a database node) is grafted under simple-login. It splits work one developer owns across two nodes, or gives one developer's database a node of its own, against the root's who-builds-what axis.

options.label: structural
options.consequence: A shape stop: the tree is re-cut (for example by feature: login and booking, each full-stack). The owner answers before anything is planned.

why: The root's decomposition axis is who builds what: the backend developer builds the service, the frontend developer builds the web app, and the integration node runs both. PRD v2 Team and delivery keeps exactly that split and adds that the backend developer owns the database, and the owner's facts repeat it and keep the integration node as the place where both run together. So rooms, bookings and PostgreSQL land in simple-login.backend, the Rooms screen and my bookings in simple-login.web, and the scripted success tests in simple-login.integration: several existing nodes' surfaces, joined through contracts, with no missing node and nothing wrong with the shape. Each leaf-parent still has one owner who can hold its scope and splits into review-sized phases, so none needs to become internal. A third developer, or a booking feature owned by a different team, would have made new-capability or structural the leading option.

question: Which new contract or contracts carry PRD v2 US-4 to US-6 across the backend to web seam?

options.label: one contract, booking-api@v1
options.consequence: One file, schema and fixture set for the rooms on a date, booking, my bookings and cancelling. The booking shape is defined once and versions once. A change to the rooms view alone still bumps the whole contract.

options.label: two contracts, room-api@v1 and booking-api@v1
options.consequence: The read view (rooms with their bookings on a date) and the write side (book, my bookings, cancel) version separately, following the auth-api and profile-api split. The booking shape appears in both, so a change to it bumps two contracts in step.

why: Both options have the same producer (simple-login.backend) and the same consumers (simple-login.web and simple-login.integration). The rooms view of AC-4.2 and AC-4.3, my bookings of AC-6.1 and the conflict message of AC-5.3 all show the same booking (room, title, start, end), so a split would define that shape twice and force lockstep bumps under hsdd-contract's per-version rules. Rooms are pre-loaded and never managed in the app (PRD v2 Rooms, Scope), so they have no lifecycle of their own to version apart. The auth-api and profile-api split does not transfer: those carry disjoint shapes. If rooms were managed in the app, or a consumer read rooms without bookings, the split would lead.
evidence: PRD v2 AC-4.1 to AC-4.3, AC-5.3, AC-6.1

question: How does the user's time zone (PRD v2 AC-2.1, AC-2.5) reach the web app: a touch of profile-api@v2 or a new profile-api version?

options.label: contract-touch on profile-api.v2
options.consequence: hsdd-contract amends v2 in place under its additive-only rule: timeZone joins the schema as an optional field and the me-ayu and me-budi fixtures carry it. Consumers that ignore unknown fields keep working; no migration window, no deprecation of v2.

options.label: contract on profile-api.v3
options.consequence: A new version with timeZone required, its own schema and fixtures, a migration mode, and profile-api@v2 deprecated or coexisting. Every node naming profile-api@v2 gets a citation move and a migration phase.

why: profile-api@v2 declares compatibility additive-only, and its own Guarantees and Versioning say it may later gain optional fields and that a later optional field keeps v2; hsdd-contract allows that only when the existing fixtures still pass against the changed schema, which an optional field satisfies. The contract's own rule therefore leads. The touch step classifies the change itself; if it finds that consumers must be able to rely on timeZone being present in every profile, which an optional field cannot promise, it classifies the change as breaking and the bump follows from there.
evidence: PRD v2 AC-2.1, AC-2.5, Demo accounts

question: Where is 'whether signing in survives a restart of the service, now that a database exists' (PRD v2 Left to engineering) decided?

options.label: adr-update on ADR-001
options.consequence: hsdd-adr revisits the session model across backend, web and the contracts that take the token: an amendment if the store stays in memory, a superseding ADR if it moves into PostgreSQL. ADR-001's Context, which rests on PRD 1's no database and two endpoints, is brought up to date in the same step.

options.label: backend D{n} in its appended phase plan
options.consequence: The backend decides alone and emits amends; ADR-001 keeps stating that restarting signs everyone out and that there is no database, which PRD v2 makes false, and the web and integration nodes learn of the change only through reconcile.

why: ADR-001 is the accepted decision for the session store, binds backend, web and both token-taking contracts, and lists 'Restarting the backend signs every user out' among its consequences; its Context cites the two-endpoint API and the ruled-out database. Changing or reaffirming the store is therefore ADR-001's to record, per hsdd-adr's ADR or D{n} table. The answer also reaches the integration node: simple-login.integration.2 uses a backend restart as its expired-token stand-in for AC-2.3, which only works while sessions die on restart, so the prompt names it. The same step decides whether sign-out stays client-side now that the endpoint count is no longer fixed.

question: Does the time handling PRD v2 asks for (AC-2.5, AC-4.2 to AC-4.4, AC-5.2, AC-5.3, AC-5.5, AC-6.2) get an ADR, or is it left to the contracts and node-local decisions?

options.label: new ADR-002, the time model
options.consequence: One accepted record says how instants travel and are stored, where the user's IANA zone comes from, which node turns a date in the user's zone into a range and formats times, which clock decides 'already started', and how clock changes stay right. booking-api, profile-api and three nodes cite it.

options.label: contracts and D{n} only
options.consequence: booking-api states its wire format; each node decides conversion and formatting locally. The rule that holds the nodes together (which side converts, which clock is authoritative) has no single home and is re-derived by each planner.

why: The decision spans simple-login.backend (storage, the day range, the 'already started' check), simple-login.web (display in the user's zone, the conflict message of AC-5.3), simple-login.integration (London's clock-change days, AC-4.4) and two contracts (profile-api's time zone, booking-api's times). hsdd-adr records a decision that affects more than one node or contract as an ADR. The ADR says why; booking-api and profile-api say what, per hsdd-adr. If only the backend handled time and the web displayed preformatted strings, a D{n} would have sufficed.
evidence: PRD v2 Goal, AC-2.5, AC-4.2 to AC-4.4, AC-5.2, AC-5.3, AC-5.5, AC-6.2

question: Does persistence in PostgreSQL 17 (PRD v2 Constraints) get an ADR of its own?

options.label: no ADR: a root hard constraint plus backend D{n}
options.consequence: The root states PostgreSQL 17 under Docker Compose as a hard constraint from PRD v2; the driver, schema, migrations and the overlap guard behind AC-5.4 are the backend's D{n}; the integration node reaches the database only through the running service, as it reaches the service today.

options.label: ADR-003, persistence
options.consequence: A third ADR records a choice the PRD already made, plus how the database is started for tests and dev; backend and integration cite it. One more binding record to keep current.

chosen: no ADR: a root hard constraint plus backend D{n}
why: PostgreSQL 17 under Docker Compose is a product constraint, not an engineering choice, so it belongs with the root's hard constraints, the way 'no database' did under PRD 1. The owner's facts and PRD v2 Team and delivery give the database to the backend developer, so what is chosen about it (driver, schema, migrations, how exactly-one-wins is enforced) dies with simple-login.backend and is a D{n} by hsdd-adr's table. Which sessions live there is ADR-001's (DEC-008). If a later planner finds the integration node must reach the database directly (to seed or reset bookings) rather than through the service or a backend script, the choice becomes cross-node and an ADR would lead.

question: Where are the longest booking and how far ahead a room can be booked (PRD v2 Left to engineering) decided?

options.label: in booking-api@v1's draft
options.consequence: hsdd-contract decides whether each limit exists and states it with its error code, so the web's form and messages and the backend's validation build against the same rule from the first draft.

options.label: in the backend's appended phase plan, emitted as amends
options.consequence: The producer decides after the contract is drafted; the contract changes again at the backend's reconcile, and the web plans against whatever the reconcile left.

why: Either limit, if it exists, is visible to consumers: a request beyond it is refused with an error the web must show and the integration tests must exercise. Consumer-visible rules belong in the contract, and drafting them there avoids an amend at the backend's reconcile. PRD v2 says engineering decides and says what it chose, so the contract's text is also where the choice is stated.
evidence: hsdd/contract/auth-api.md Guarantees / invariants (consumers branch on error.code)

question: With a third screen (Rooms, PRD v2 Screens), where is the web app's navigation decided, given RFC-001 §6 and the web's D4 'No router'?

options.label: web D4, revisited in its appended phase plan
options.consequence: simple-login.web decides between a session-and-screen state value and a router; the integration node is unaffected because its selectors stay on visible text.

options.label: an ADR
options.consequence: A tree-level record for a choice only one node implements; ADRs stop being few.

chosen: web D4, revisited in its appended phase plan
why: RFC-001 §6 made 'no router' a frontend-stack choice and the web plan holds it as D4; no other node or contract depends on how the web app moves between screens, since simple-login.integration's browser tests select by visible text. hsdd-adr records a decision internal to one node as a D{n}. The web spec touch only stops saying 'two screens'.
evidence: hsdd/spec/simple-login.integration.md simple-login.integration.2 Scope (selectors stay on visible text)

question: RFC-001 (normative, read-only) still says the service owns accounts and sessions in memory, the API has two endpoints, restarting signs everybody out because there is no database, and two screens need no router; PRD v2 overtakes each. How are these statements resolved?

options.label: resolve locally, flag upstream
options.consequence: The tree records the new technical approach in ADR-001's update, ADR-002, booking-api@v1, the root's hard constraints and the web's D4; RFC-001 stays as written and the decision is flagged so the developers can amend it or write an RFC for version 2.

options.label: stop for the team's RFC
options.consequence: The run waits for the developers to write the technical approach for version 2 outside the repository; nothing is planned until then.

why: DEC-001 kept RFC-001 normative because its sign-in, password and stack choices still hold, and noted that its database and endpoint statements follow from PRD 1's scope, which PRD v2 replaces. The run's policy resolves a read-only source's stale statements locally. Each stale statement already has a home in this record's handoffs: sessions and sign-out in ADR-001's update (DEC-008), times in ADR-002 (DEC-009), the endpoints in booking-api@v1 (DEC-006), the database in the root's constraints (DEC-010), the router in web D4 (DEC-012). The right final fix is upstream: RFC-001 describes version 1 only, and its authors own the technical approach. A careful engineer would tell the two developers before overriding their accepted RFC in ADRs.
evidence: PRD v2 Constraints, Scope, Left to engineering

question: Which nodes take a spec-touch for a change to their own text (not for contract versions in their headers, which reconcile writes)?

options.label: the root and all three leaf-parents
options.consequence: Four touches: the root's purpose, ownership, hard constraints and decisions; each child's Purpose, Owns, Isolation strategy and Overview, with the root's embedded summary of it. Every node's header says what it now does before its phases are appended.

options.label: the root, backend and web only
options.consequence: Three touches; the integration node's Owns and Isolation strategy keep saying it runs the service and the web app and drives a browser, while its new phases also run PostgreSQL and HTTP-level concurrency and restart tests.

options.label: the root only
options.consequence: One touch; the leaf-parents' headers stay at version 1 scope and their appended phases describe work their Purpose and Owns lines do not cover. Append mode cannot fix those lines.

chosen: the root and all three leaf-parents
why: The root's text is false under PRD v2 (no database, exactly two endpoints, persistence not owned). simple-login.backend's Purpose and Owns lack rooms, bookings and the database, and its Isolation strategy ('no open port needed') must say bookings tests run against a real PostgreSQL (PRD v2 Constraints). simple-login.web's Purpose, Owns and Overview ('Two screens and no router') lack the Rooms screen and my bookings. simple-login.integration's Owns names only a browser test, while PRD v2 Success adds 20 simultaneous booking attempts and a restart that keeps bookings, which it runs against the real service with its database. Append mode never edits a node header's lines other than Sources, so only a touch fixes them. The integration touch is the closest call; had PRD v2 Success been coverable by browser tests alone, it would have been dropped.

question: Which artifacts get a citation-touch handoff (when: cites-superseded) for the move from PRD 1 and Update 1 to PRD v2?

options.label: the four node specs only
options.consequence: Four touches, each over a file that cites hsdd/context/prd-simple-login.md and hsdd/context/update-1-add-phone.md in Sources (and 'update 1' in prose). ADR-001's and profile-api@v2's real references to the old PRD are rewritten by their own content handoffs.

options.label: the four node specs plus auth-api, profile-api and ADR-001
options.consequence: Seven touches. The condition holds for auth-api and profile-api only because the baseline version token '1' matches numbers such as '1 to 64 characters' and minLength 1, so those two dispatch a subagent each that moves nothing; ADR-001's would be skipped.

why: The experiment ran the run's own cites-superseded code over every candidate. On the four specs the condition holds through real citations of both baseline paths. On auth-api, profile-api and profile-api.v2 it holds only on numbers, which are not citations; on ADR-001 it does not hold. The two real prose references outside the specs, ADR-001's 'The PRD needs' context and profile-api@v2's 'matches the change request', sit in files that H1 and H5 rewrite for content. No contract version is superseded at this point (profile-api@v1 is still stable), so no contract-version citation needs moving; the insert rule covers a version that becomes superseded during the segment.

question: No intake record is open, but the open 2026-10-30 execution plan has governance repairs on the files this intake touches (C-1 deprecate profile-api@v1 after Sync A's A-1, C-2 add simple-login to ADR-001's affects, C-3 complete auth-api@v1's consumers). Does this record absorb them?

options.label: leave them to the execution plan; route consider items to H1, H4 and H5
options.consequence: The steps editing ADR-001, auth-api and profile-api@v2 see the pending repairs and may fix the two pure link fixes (C-2, C-3) while there, citing them; C-1 stays with the owner's Sync A decision on the sunset date and is not pre-empted. No collision line, since neither is an intake.

options.label: add handoffs for C-1 to C-3
options.consequence: This intake also deprecates profile-api@v1 and fixes the two links; it takes A-1's sunset decision away from the owner's sync on 2026-11-02 and mixes another plan's repairs into this request's ledger.

chosen: leave them to the execution plan; route consider items to H1, H4 and H5
why: hsdd-intake's collision rules cover open intake records only, and the one earlier record is closed, so Collisions is none. The execution plan's C-1 waits on A-1, a decision the owner takes at Sync A, so this run must not deprecate profile-api@v1; C-2 and C-3 are link fixes with no dependency that the steps touching those files can absorb without deciding anything new. Routing them as consider items lets those steps choose and record it, and keeps this record's ledger to PRD v2.
evidence: hsdd/management/2026-10-30-execution-plan.md Sync A A-1, Step tables C-1 to C-3

question: S02's report lists 21 reads outside its inputs (the open execution plan, the run's own records, conventions, the other planning skills, hsdd-auto's scripts, schemas and step templates). Keep the output or rework?

options.label: Keep the output
options.consequence: The intake record stands; the reads are recorded in the report for the owner's review.

options.label: Rework without those reads
options.consequence: A second pass of the same routing with less information about the receiving skills' forms and the gate's checks; the record would likely be the same or weaker.

why: Every read is of a file inside the repository that a careful router would consult: the open execution plan for collisions, the receiving skills to phrase their prompts, and the run's own scripts to place handoffs and conditions correctly. None is an out-of-bounds path, none carries a fact the step should not have used, and each why names what it was for. A read of another project or of agent memory would have changed this choice.
